questions.title: Why does DeepSeekMath use a fastText classifier for selecting Common Crawl pages, and how does it avoid overfitting to the initial seed corpus?
questions.question_body: In the data collection pipeline, the authors train a fastText model on 500k positive OpenWebMath examples and 500k negative Common Crawl pages. They then use this model to recall more math pages, rank them, and keep the top ones. How does this iterative approach prevent the model from learning only the narrow style of the seed corpus? What mechanisms are in place to ensure diversity in the retrieved pages across iterations?

questions.title: What is the role of URL-based deduplication and near-deduplication before applying fastText, and how does it affect the token count?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions deduplication techniques that reduce the Common Crawl size before training fastText. How exactly do these techniques work (e.g., hashing, shingling), and how do they influence the final 40–120B token count reported? Do they remove entire domains or only duplicate documents?

questions.title: How does DeepSeekMath ensure that benchmark contamination is avoided when filtering extracted web pages?
questions.question_body: The authors filter out any 10‑gram substring that appears in GSM8K, MATH, CMATH, or AGIEval. What happens if a benchmark problem contains a unique phrase fewer than 10 grams but appears multiple times across other dumps? Also, how are short prompts (<10 grams) handled differently?

questions.title: Why does incorporating code tokens during pre‑training improve mathematical reasoning even without tool use?
questions.question_body: Table 5 shows that a two‑stage pipeline (400B code → 150B math) yields better performance on no‑tool CoT tasks than one‑stage (400B code + 150B math). What linguistic or structural properties of code help models learn arithmetic or algebraic patterns that general language training does not provide?

questions.title: What is meant by “baseline from group scores” in GRPO and how is it computed?
questions.question_body:
"Baseline” usually refers to a value function in actor‑critic algorithms. In GRPO they say it is estimated from group scores. Does this mean simply taking 
\(\hat A_{i,t} = \frac{r_i- \bar r}{\sigma}\) for each token in a sampled group 
\(\{o_1,…,o_G\}\)? How does this compare to using a learned value network like PPO?

questions.title: How are group reward statistics used when computing advantages for individual tokens in GRPO?
questions.question_body: In outcome supervision GRPO sets \(\hat A_{i,t}=\tilde r_i\) for every token in an output. In process supervision it sums normalized step rewards from token t onward. Could you walk through an example with two outputs of different lengths and show exactly how \(\hat A_{i,t}\) changes at each token?

questions.title: `KL divergence estimator` in equation (4) seems non‑standard – why not use the usual cross‑entropy form?
questions.question_body: "Equation 4 provides an unbiased estimator: \(D_{KL}= r_ref/r_θ - log(r_ref/r_θ)-1\). Why choose this form instead of computing \(E_{ref}[log π_ref - log π_θ]\)? Does this have numerical stability advantages when sampling multiple outputs with different lengths?

questions.title: Why does REJECT Sampling Fine‑Tuning (RFT) underperform online RFT in their experiments?
questions.question_body: "Observations about Data Source" state that online RFT surpasses offline RFT because real‑time sampling yields more diverse data. However, both refer to sampling from an SFT policy. Is the difference only in when sampling occurs, or are there differences in how correct answers are selected or filtered after sampling?

questions.title: How does GRPO avoid over‑optimization of irrelevant tokens when using only final‑token rewards?
questions.question_body: "Outcome supervision only provides a reward at the end of each output" – yet GRPO applies advantage to every token via its min/clipping operator. Are there occasions where tokens before the final one receive disproportionate updates because their probabilities were correlated with the reward? Would adding per‑token minimal reward signals help?

questions.title: `Process supervision` seems computationally heavier – how is it implemented efficiently?
questions.question_body: "Process supervision provides a reward at each reasoning step" and then sums normalized rewards for all tokens after a step. For long solutions (e.g., >1000 tokens), doesn’t computing per‑step rewards blow up memory? Does DeepSeekMath evaluate step boundaries on-the-fly or batch them across examples?

questions.title: "Iterative RL" uses a replay buffer with 10% historical data – why such a small fraction?
questions.question_body: "In iterative GRPO we generate new training sets for the reward model using samples from the current policy" but only keep 10% past data. What evidence suggests that 10% suffices to prevent catastrophic forgetting of earlier preferences vs. higher ratios which might slow convergence?

questions.title: "ArXiv papers seem ineffective” – could data quality be the culprit?
questions.question_body: - The authors say models trained on arXiv‐only corpora ‘display no notable improvements or even deterioration’. Is this due to tokenization problems (macros, citations) or because arXiv texts are too formal/labeled? Is there evidence that cleaning arXiv LaTeX would improve mathematical reasoning?

questions.title: `42% accuracy on MATH initial results vs 51.7% after GRPO` – what drives this numeric jump?
questions.question_body: "Table 6 shows DeepSeekMath‑RL reaches 51.7% on MATH versus 46.8% after Instruct tuning". Can we attribute this improvement purely to better answer ranking (Maj@K boost shown in Fig 8), or does GRPO actually increase correct reasoning steps? How would you measure this empirically?
